what_its_for: Cisplatin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat several types of cancer, including bladder cancer, testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, and other solid tumors. It works by damaging the DNA inside cancer cells, which stops them from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: Cisplatin is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a nurse or doctor in a hospital or infusion clinic. You will NOT take this medicine at home by mouth. Each infusion session usually takes several hours. You will also receive IV fluids before and after your cisplatin infusion to help protect your kidneys. It is very important to drink plenty of water and fluids on the days around your treatment unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your height, weight, kidney function, and the type of cancer being treated. Doses are usually given once every 3 to 4 weeks, or sometimes once daily for several days in a row followed by a rest period. Never try to adjust your dose on your own. Your medical team will monitor your blood counts and kidney function regularly and may change your dose if needed.
missed_dose: Because cisplatin is given by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital, a missed dose is uncommon. However, if you miss or need to reschedule your appointment, call your oncology team right away. Do not try to make up a dose on your own. Your doctor will decide the best time to give your next treatment.
storage: Cisplatin is stored and handled by trained pharmacy staff. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you are given any take-home medicines as part of your cancer care (such as anti-nausea pills), store those as directed on the label, usually at room temperature away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids as directed by your care team. Avoid taking aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other anti-inflammatory pain relievers unless your doctor approves, as they can put extra stress on your kidneys. Avoid live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax) during treatment. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, since cisplatin can lower your immune system. Avoid alcohol or ask your doctor if it is safe. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, especially aminoglycoside antibiotics (like gentamicin) and water pills (diuretics), which can increase the risk of kidney or hearing problems.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to an emergency room right away if you experience: decreased urination or no urination at all (possible kidney problem); ringing in the ears, hearing loss, or muffled sounds; severe nausea, vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down; numbness, tingling, or burning in your hands or feet; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or shaking; unusual bleeding or bruising; severe dizziness or balance problems; swelling in your legs or ankles; or muscle cramps and weakness. Contact your care team for any new or worsening symptoms between treatments.
when_it_works: Cisplatin begins working right away at the cellular level during your infusion, but it may take several weeks or multiple treatment cycles before you or your doctor can see the full benefit. Your doctor will check your response to treatment through scans, blood tests, and physical exams throughout your treatment course. Do not get discouraged if you do not feel better right away — the effects build over time.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Cisplatin can be very hard on the kidneys. Your kidney function will be tested before every cycle. Your dose may be reduced or your treatment delayed if your kidneys are not working well. Drinking enough fluids and receiving IV hydration helps protect your kidneys. Hearing problems: Cisplatin can cause permanent hearing loss, especially at high frequencies. Hearing tests may be done before and during treatment, especially in children and older adults. Children and young patients: Cisplatin is used in children for certain cancers, but hearing loss risk is higher in this age group and will be closely monitored. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to kidney damage, nerve damage, and hearing loss. Doses may be adjusted accordingly. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Cisplatin can seriously harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for some time after. Do not breastfeed while receiving cisplatin. Men should also use contraception and discuss fertility preservation with their doctor before starting treatment.
